question:
A class examines the inverse of a square matrix using the definition based on matrix multiplication. They are given $A=\begin{bmatrix}2&3\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{bmatrix}2&-3\\-1&2\end{bmatrix}$. The teacher explains that a square matrix is invertible when another matrix of the same order multiplies with it on either side to give the identity matrix. After checking whether $B$ provides such a matrix for $A$, the students consider a hypothetical matrix $C$ that is also claimed to be an inverse of $A$. They must then use the associative property and the identity matrix to examine whether two different inverses of the same matrix can exist.

(a) Calculate $AB$.

(b) Calculate $BA$ and hence determine whether the inverse of $A$ exists and identify it.

(c) Suppose $C$ is also an inverse of $A$. Using the inverse relations and associativity of matrix multiplication, show that $B=C$.

(d) Determine whether $B$ is invertible and identify $B^{-1}$. Justify your conclusion.
explanation:
(a)
Using row-by-column multiplication, $AB=\begin{bmatrix}2&3\\1&2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2&-3\\-1&2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4-3&-6+6\\2-2&-3+4\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}=I$.

(b)
Similarly, $BA=\begin{bmatrix}2&-3\\-1&2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2&3\\1&2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4-3&6-6\\-2+2&-3+4\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}=I$. Since both $AB=I$ and $BA=I$, matrix $B$ is the inverse of $A$. Therefore, $A$ is invertible, the inverse exists, and $A^{-1}=B=\begin{bmatrix}2&-3\\-1&2\end{bmatrix}$.

(c)
If $C$ is also an inverse of $A$, then $AC=CA=I$. Since $B$ is an inverse of $A$, $BA=AB=I$. Now, $B=BI=B(AC)$. By associativity of matrix multiplication, $B(AC)=(BA)C$. Since $BA=I$, $(BA)C=IC=C$. Therefore, $B=C$. Hence, the inverse of a square matrix, if it exists, is unique.

(d)
From parts (a) and (b), $BA=AB=I$. Thus, $A$ is also an inverse of $B$. Therefore, $B$ is invertible and $B^{-1}=A=\begin{bmatrix}2&3\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$. This follows directly from the fact that two matrices whose products in both orders equal the identity matrix are inverses of each other.

options.A:
(a) $AB=I$.
(b) $BA=I$, so $A^{-1}=B$.
(c) If $C$ is another inverse, $B=C$ by associativity.
(d) $B$ is not invertible because only $A$ has an inverse.
options.B:
(a) $AB=I$.
(b) $BA\ne I$, so $B$ is only a right inverse of $A$.
(c) Two different inverses of $A$ may exist.
(d) $B^{-1}=A$.
options.C:
(a) $AB=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$.
(b) $BA=I$, so $A^{-1}=B$.
(c) If $C$ is another inverse, then $B=-C$.
(d) $B^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}2&-3\\-1&2\end{bmatrix}$.
options.D:
(a) $AB=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}=I$.
(b) $BA=I$, hence $A$ is invertible and $A^{-1}=B=\begin{bmatrix}2&-3\\-1&2\end{bmatrix}$.
(c) If $C$ is also an inverse, then $B=BI=B(AC)=(BA)C=IC=C$, so the inverse is unique.
(d) $B$ is invertible and $B^{-1}=A=\begin{bmatrix}2&3\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$.
